Xinhua world news summary at 1530 GMT, Nov. 4
text: WASHINGTON -- Democrats are projected to flip control of the U.S. Senate after winning several key races in battleground states, securing control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, election forecasting agency Decision Desk HQ reported late Tuesday.

Before the midterms, Republicans held 218 seats in the House of Representatives, compared with 214 for Democrats. The chamber also had one independent member and two vacancies, one in a Republican-held district and the other in a Democratic-held district, following the resignations of their respective representatives in 2026. (US-Midterms)

SEOUL -- Former South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol faces possible invalidation of his 2022 election as an appellate court on Wednesday upheld a suspended prison sentence for election law violations linked to false statements during his presidential campaign.

The Seoul High Court sentenced Yoon to one and a half years in prison, suspended for three years, dismissing his appeal and upholding the lower court's guilty verdict on all counts of violating the public official election law. (South Korea-Former President-Election)

JERUSALEM -- Israel's Central Elections Committee officially announced the results of last week's parliamentary election on Wednesday, confirming that opposition parties won 67 seats in the 120-member parliament, against 53 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's ruling bloc.

The opposition's 67 seats include 48 won by parties aligned with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party and 19 by the Arab-led parties, namely the Joint List, a coalition of three parties, and the Muslim Ra'am party. (Israel-Election Results)

JOHANNESBURG -- South Africa's local government elections kicked off on Wednesday as voting officially opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT), with more than 29 million registered voters expected to cast their ballots at nearly 23,700 polling stations across the country.

Polling stations are scheduled to close at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT), with final results to be announced after the Independent Electoral Commission completes the counting and verification process. (South Africa-Municipal Elections)  ■

items.title: News Analysis: Israeli election exposes limits of political change amid divisions over Arab parties
text: JERUSALEM, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- Israel's parliamentary election has stripped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing alliance of its majority, but the refusal of most of his Jewish opponents to rely on Arab parties could keep him in power, exposing the limits of political change, analysts say.

Official results released Wednesday showed Netanyahu's bloc falling from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-member parliament. Parties opposed to him secured 67 seats, including a record 19 won by two Arab-led parties, namely the Joint List, a coalition of three parties, and the Muslim Ra'am party.

Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's four-party alliance holds 48 seats. Of the four parties, three reject Arab support, while the left-wing Democrats advocate cooperation, leaving the anti-Netanyahu majority without an agreed path to power.

The Joint List won 11 seats and Ra'am eight, nearly doubling their combined 10 seats in the outgoing parliament. Voter turnout in Arab localities surged to about 77 percent from 53.2 percent in 2022, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a think tank.

Eyal Zisser, a professor at Tel Aviv University, told Xinhua the surge reflected hostility toward the outgoing government -- a coalition of right-wing, pro-settler and ultra-Orthodox parties -- and a desire for greater political influence.
"They want to remove Netanyahu from office and to remove this government from office," he said.
Arab citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are largely Palestinians who remained after the 1948 war and their descendants.

Reda Jaber, a researcher specializing in law and Arab politics in Israel, told Xinhua that Arab voters sought to assert their citizenship against discriminatory policies, including restrictions on political activity, home demolitions and rising crime.
Yet most Jewish opposition leaders reject cooperation with Arab parties despite their offers to help replace Netanyahu.

Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen told CNN his alliance would act as a "safety net" for a new government, supporting it from outside to oust Netanyahu. He cited Arab parties' backing of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin's government in the 1990s, which provided the majority needed to advance the Oslo peace accords with the Palestinians.
Jabareen called on opposition leaders to follow Rabin's example, saying cooperation with Arab parties could open "a new direction in Israeli politics."
Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas, whose party joined the coalition that ousted Netanyahu in 2021, has explicitly expressed willingness to join an Eisenkot-led government.

Jaber argued that the opposition's refusal reflected deeper barriers to Arab political influence. Israel, he said, has "no liberal bloc willing or able to expand the scope of citizenship to include Arabs." Continued exclusion could alienate Arab voters in the next elections and benefit Netanyahu's camp, he warned.
CHANGE OF LEADERSHIP, NOT NECESSARILY POLICY

items.title: News Analysis: South African municipal polls test ANC dominance amid growing coalition politics
text: JOHANNESBURG, Nov. 4 (Xinhua) -- Millions of South Africans head to the polls on Wednesday for municipal elections that will serve as a crucial test of support for the ruling African National Congress (ANC). As opposition parties seek to expand their foothold, local governance across the country is increasingly defined by complex coalition dynamics.

The elections take place amid mounting public anger over failing municipal services, high unemployment, corruption, and deteriorating infrastructure. They also mark a major electoral trial since the ANC lost its absolute parliamentary majority in the May 2024 general elections, a watershed moment in South Africa's post-apartheid political evolution.
The elections will hinge largely on municipal performance, as residents assess whether local administrations have delivered on their commitments to provide basic services and maintain infrastructure.
In major economic hubs, chronic water scarcity, frequent power disruptions, neglected road networks, and municipal financial mismanagement have dominated voters' concerns.

Johannesburg, the country's economic center, faces severe pressure over aging infrastructure and systemic water losses. Other key metropolitan areas, such as Tshwane and eThekwini, face similar strain alongside soaring unemployment and fiscal distress.
Data from Statistics South Africa for the second quarter of 2026 underscores the crisis, with unemployment rates standing at 35.9 percent in Johannesburg and 34.2 percent in Tshwane.

Economic hardship has fueled widespread skepticism toward political leadership. A pre-election Ipsos survey revealed that 68 percent of registered voters distrust politicians, while half feel unrepresented by any political party.

Rather than consolidating support behind a single opposition alternative, voter dissatisfaction has driven political fragmentation. The electorate is increasingly polarized and, in many cases, alienated from the political process altogether.
The fiercest contests are expected in the country's eight metropolitan municipalities: Buffalo, Cape Town, Ekurhuleni, eThekwini, Johannesburg, Mangaung, Nelson Mandela Bay, and Tshwane.

Major party players, including the ANC, the Democratic Alliance, the uMkhonto weSizwe Party, the Economic Freedom Fighters, the Inkatha Freedom Party, and ActionSA, are vying to consolidate their influence.
With Ipsos projections suggesting no single party will secure absolute majorities in key metros, intense post-election bargaining is widely expected.

While the ANC's entry into a Government of National Unity at the federal level following the 2024 elections brought former rivals together, local-level coalitions operate under far more volatile conditions.
For voters, the overriding concern is whether these political pacts can deliver stable governance rather than merely serve as vehicles for political patronage.

Wednesday's vote will provide a critical barometer of the ANC's political trajectory following its 2024 setback and test whether opposition forces can convert public discontent into lasting local governance.

Australian businesses tap Shenzhen
text: For Australian aromatherapy entrepreneur Adam Good, taking his startup to Chinese technology hub Shenzhen is the logical leap toward success.

"In Australia, we believe that nature and plant-based botanicals are important. When we came to the precision, hardware requirements, the ability to get good tooling, (and) software integration, we went to Shenzhen," said the co-founder and CEO of Auric, a wellness startup that taps artificial intelligence for aromatherapy systems.

Good said his products such as essential oils leverage Australia's high standards in premium natural ingredients, and complements a flagship device that dispenses scents through digital advances like mobile apps.

"It's made with manufacturing partners in Shenzhen, at a speed and cost we could not match anywhere else", with the high-tech consumer market there also offering an ideal platform for developing the product, he said.
In December, Good will be heading to the city in South China's Guangdong province, home to tech giants like Tencent and Huawei, to continue building his business and partnerships.
The entrepreneur was speaking at the Sydney session of the 2026 Shenzhen Global Investment Promotion Conference on Nov 4.

The conference, sponsored by the Shenzhen municipality and organized by its investment promotion bureau, showcased the city's strengths in innovation and investment to the Australian business community as it promotes high-quality growth in line with the latest development priorities.
The Shenzhen Economic and Trade Office, or SETO, in Australia, a business service provider representing the city, co-organized the Sydney session with investment promotion agency Invest Hong Kong.

At the event, more than 80 representatives from local government, enterprises, universities, innovation incubators, industry associations and other institutions gathered to further explore economic and trade-exchange opportunities, and cooperation between China and Australia.

The trade office highlighted Shenzhen's strengths and achievements, including its top ranking among Chinese mainland cities for exports in the past three decades, with total goods imports and exports hitting A$986 billion ($691 billion) last year.
Australia is Shenzhen's largest trading partner in the Southern Hemisphere, with trade in goods between the two recording A$14.8 billion last year.

The city is also looking to strengthen its role in driving the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and position itself as a premier global investment destination, according to the conference organizers. Major areas of development include leading industrial clusters and the services industry.

Session participants were also presented with the latest economic, business and trade trends, and opportunities in the run-up to Shenzhen hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation global meetings later this month.
Wang Sisi, consul, economic and commercial office, at the Chinese Consulate-General in Sydney, highlighted the shared development focus on openness, innovation and cooperation.
Shenzhen, known as China's "Silicon Valley", is a major hub for high-tech industries and manufacturing, she said.

items.title: Bayer attends CIIE for the ninth consecutive year with nearly 30 debuts, harnessing life science innovation to serve China and connect the world
text: The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) opened today in Shanghai. A full-attendance exhibitor for nine consecutive years, Bayer is once again bringing together its Pharmaceuticals (including Radiology), Consumer Health and Crop Science divisions to showcase global innovations and the latest local practices in healthcare and modern agriculture. At this year's CIIE, Bayer has a dual presence at Booth A3-03 in the Medical Equipment & Healthcare Products Exhibition Area of Hall 1.1 and Booth B3-02 in the Food and Agricultural Products Exhibition Area of Hall 8.1. The company is presenting nearly 30 debuts spanning disease treatment and precision diagnostics, everyday self-care, and enhanced quality and efficiency in agriculture. Through the CIIE, Bayer is not only accelerating the introduction of global innovations to China but also helping integrate China's needs and local insights into its global R&D network, using life science innovation to connect China with the world.

Bill Anderson, chairman of the board of management of Bayer AG, remarks: "For Bayer, the CIIE is more than an exhibition. It is where people come together to exchange ideas, build partnerships, and turn innovation into real-world impact. The world faces big challenges, from improving health outcomes for growing and aging populations to producing enough food in a responsible way. No company or country can solve them alone. Progress requires openness, collaboration, and innovation. The CIIE makes that possible by bringing together partners from across industries and around the world. With more than 160 years of experience, our mission remains clear 'Health for all, Hunger for none'. We look forward to working with partners across the innovation ecosystem, and by connecting local expertise with our global capabilities we're determined to build a healthier, more resilient future. Next year will be especially meaningful as Bayer marks 145 years in China. Few companies have been part of China's development journey for that long, and it is something we are proud of, and we look forward to continuing this journey together."

HK activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years behind bars
text: Joshua Wong Chi-fung, an instigator of anti-China riots, was sentenced to 10 years under the National Security Law of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region on Thursday for persistently calling for foreign sanctions on China (including the HKSAR) after the law's promulgation on June 30, 2020, with two months and two days run concurrently for another offense in another case.

National security judge William Tam Yiu-ho first set the penalty at 13 years, then reduced it to 10 years considering Wong's plea and mitigation, the minimum term for an offense "of a grave nature" under the NSL of HKSAR.

Wong, the former secretary-general of the now-disbanded political party Demosisto and who is already serving a prison sentence for subversion, pleaded guilty in the High Court on Sept 2 to the count of colluding with foreign entities, conspiring with his party mate, fugitive former legislator Nathan Law Kwun-chung, and others in Hong Kong to seek support from the international community to impose sanctions, blockades, or other hostile actions against mainland and Hong Kong between July 1, 2020, and Nov 23, 2020.

"The punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed. It is also necessary for the court to express the community's abhorrence of the defendant's scheme and acts together with others to collude with foreign forces or external elements to endanger national security, and to serve the imperative of deterrence," Tam said while handing down the penalty.
Contact the writer at stacyshi@chinadailyhk.com

Chinese enterprises explore new pathways for global energy transition
text: Academics, industry executives and international partners gathered in Shanghai on Saturday to discuss clean energy transformation and corporate globalization.

The inaugural 21st century global enterprise forum, held at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, focused on strategic approaches for Chinese companies seeking to navigate the complex opportunities and challenges of expanding internationally amid an accelerated global transition toward green energy.

Zeng Yuqun, founder and CEO of CATL and honorary dean of the 21st Century Institute for Global Enterprise, delivered video remarks emphasizing the need for Chinese enterprises to share their technological innovations and industrial capabilities with the world.

"We need to bridge real-world challenges in global expansion with academic research capabilities," Zeng said. "By exploring through practice and synthesizing through research, we can provide valuable insights to guide more Chinese companies going global."

"Enterprises need to balance globalization with localization, rethinking supply chain layout and efficiency," said Ni Jun, deputy director of the Shanghai Jiao Tong University council and CATL's chief manufacturing officer. "Academia should work closely with enterprises to understand industrial practice and explore future-oriented management theories and talent cultivation models."

Chen Fangruo, dean of Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Antai College of Economics and Management and dean of the 21st Century Institute for Global Enterprise, noted that Chinese companies face new challenges overseas.

"Conventional transnational models may no longer fully apply," Chen observed. "Transitioning from exporting products to exporting systemic capabilities requires joint exploration between academia and industry."

In a keynote address on new energy developments, Huang Zhen, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, pointed out that the sector is shifting from sheer capacity growth to deep system integration and value creation.
He advocated for a deeper convergence of renewable energy with industrial manufacturing, transportation, and computing infrastructure to unlock new avenues for green transformation.
A panel discussion further examined the transition from traditional market expansion to sustainable international partnerships, analyzing changing global expectations for clean energy providers.

Prior to the public forum, the institute hosted a closed-door session on building clean energy systems, covering renewable grid integration, green finance, power-computing synergy and cross-border cooperation.

items.title: Democratic wave reshapes Washington, but policy shifts remain uncertain
text:
By YIFAN XU in Washington | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-05 12:44

Democrats' sweeping victories in Tuesday's midterm elections have shifted the balance of power in Washington, setting up two years of divided government. Analysts say the new congressional majorities will bring stronger scrutiny of President Donald Trump's administration, although their ability to change his domestic and foreign policies remains uncertain.

Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, ending unified Republican control of Washington. As of Wednesday, Democrats and independents who caucus with them had secured at least 54 Senate seats, including traditionally Republican states such as Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, while counting continued in some races. The new Congress takes office on Jan 3.
Asked about the election's implications for China-US ties, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, "The US midterm elections are a domestic affair".

Mao said China stood ready to work with the United States to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state, enhance communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation, and build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity.

"The US-China relationship is unlikely to change because of the election," said Jack Midgley, principal at Midgley & Company and adjunct associate professor at Georgetown University's Center for Security Studies.

Kenton Thibaut of the Atlantic Council, meanwhile, saw potential for congressional support for China-US coordination on artificial intelligence safety, subject to negotiations between the two governments.
In a Wednesday post-election discussion hosted by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, Daniel Drezner, a Tufts University professor, linked voters' economic concerns to foreign policy.

"Americans fundamentally do not care about foreign policy unless it affects their bottom line," he said. The discussion repeatedly returned to the impact of the Iran war and tariffs on household costs.

Justin Logan, director of defense and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute, wrote on Wednesday that the Iran war had played an unusually important electoral role because higher energy costs made its consequences visible to voters. Rebecca Patterson of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) expected the incoming Congress to prioritize affordability and corruption, including efforts to lower housing, food, energy and healthcare costs.

Midgley of Georgetown University offered a more skeptical view on Wednesday. He told China Daily that Trump's veto power and broad executive authority would limit the Democrats' ability to enact major legislation and predicted that congressional investigations could take precedence over lawmaking.

items.title: Digital path opened for China-ASEAN dental cooperation
text:
By ZHANG LI in Nanning | 
          China Daily |
          Updated: 2026-11-05 10:56

Serving as China's frontline hub for engagement with members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region is deploying artificial intelligence to overcome geographic distances and language barriers and build new digital avenues for exchanges and collaboration in stomatology between China and the region.

Kuang Hai, deputy Party secretary of the Guangxi Medical University College Hospital of Stomatology, said AI has become a key tool to advance China-ASEAN health cooperation, shifting the partnership from traditional academic visits toward a two-way, inclusive phase covering medical services and workforce development.

The hospital has long supported health collaboration with ASEAN and has hosted the China-ASEAN Forum on Dentistry for nine consecutive years. Since 1992, it has trained more than 200 dental professionals from 15 ASEAN countries and regions. Its collaborative network now stretches to medical institutions and universities across 35 countries worldwide.

As the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership took effect, regional trade and cross-border mobility have grown easier. The hospital has integrated AI across clinical care, hospital operations and cross-border training to resolve practical hurdles facing international collaboration.

Robust smart infrastructure forms the foundation for cross-border medical work. The hospital operates the first drone-powered smart logistics delivery system at a Chinese dental hospital, paired with intelligent logistics robots to create closed-loop transport for pharmaceuticals, dental supplies and clinical instruments, thus boosting operational efficiency.

AI improves care for Chinese and foreign patients alike. AI triage tools and self-service oral screening devices help patients get initial dental assessments in a timely fashion. Intelligent analysis of dental scans, AI-assisted treatment planning and dental implant robots are now part of routine clinical work.

"So far, more than 50 ASEAN patients have received treatment with our AI implant robot. This domestically developed smart medical device has been adopted by multiple facilities in Vietnam and Singapore," Kuang said.

For cleft lip and palate rehabilitation, the hospital has built an AI large language model-powered speech assessment platform for home therapy. The service has helped more than 2,000 users, letting patients in remote areas complete rehabilitation at home and cut down on repeated travel for treatment.

Language gaps and travel restrictions have long slowed cross-border learning for ASEAN dentists. The hospital has developed a proprietary multilingual AI simultaneous interpretation system for stomatology that supports real-time translation across more than 10 Southeast Asian languages, removing language barriers in seminars and technical training.

The hospital has also built an AI-plus-virtual reality simulation training ecosystem with full sets of clinical dental courses. ASEAN practitioners can complete immersive simulated training without traveling abroad by using VR headsets.

text: 【财新网】随着AI从手机应用走向机器人、智能眼镜等物理设备，未来通信网络的服务对象将从人类用户扩展至大量能够自主感知、决策和行动的AI智能体。11月4日进博会开幕前夕，瑞典通信设备供应商爱立信中国区技术部副总经理张永涛在媒体交流会上表示，这一变化将对通信网络的带宽、时延和算力资源调度能力提出新的要求。

text: 据报道，10月30日至31日举行的二十国集团外长会，未能在地缘和经济安全问题上达成共识。10月31日，美日澳印四国外长在亚特兰大举行“四方安全对话”，表示有意提供超过8500万美元技术和财政援助，支持印太地区获得“可信人工智能”；美国另承诺提供1000万美元，支持印度和东盟建设关键矿产回收设施。

text: 【财新网】香港SKYTOPIA滨水展区，国际机场的航班起落声不绝于耳，财政司司长陈茂波观赏着停泊在此的一排排超级游艇。
作为香港全新试水的首届高端生活展会，“世界鉴赏家盛典”（TFOC）11月4日正式开幕。它是政府斥资1亿港元专项拨款的首个项目，真金白银的投入，并非只为打造一场奢华展演，而是香港正主动调整财富服务模式的试探。
曾几何时，香港是内地高净值人群的奢侈品专属采购地。过去20余年，内地富人赴港消费的核心场景主要集中于珠宝、名表、皮具等实物奢侈品，香港依靠关税、汇率优势，稳坐内地高端消费的“中转站”。但这套传统商业模式在疫情后早已式微。随着内地高端商场业态完善、国际奢侈品牌布局扩大，叠加海南离岛免税政策持续扩容，两地奢侈品价差大幅收窄，曾经盛行的“跨境扫货”热潮也逐渐退去。

text: 【财新网】远景科技集团乌兰察布数据中心一期约200兆瓦（MW）项目已于2026年10月底整体向客户交付。第二期同等规模项目预计于2027年第二季度投产。远景计划，到2027年底或2028年初，在三、四期项目建设完成后，整体园区的算力规模达到1吉瓦（GW，1GW=1000MW）。
远景科技集团AIDC（人工智能算力中心）总经理郑子浩10月下旬在接受财新专访时表示。
在乌兰察布察哈尔高新技术开发区，远景人工智能算力产业园一期工程项目包含一栋算力中心、一栋综合运维楼及一座220千伏变电站。

items.title: China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019224/China Vows to Share Its Market With the World at 9th Annual CIIE
text: Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang pledged to share China’s market with the rest of the world and promote balanced international economic development at the opening ceremony of the 2026 China International Import Expo (CIIE) on Thursday.
“Mutual benefit is at the heart of trade and economic cooperation,” Ding said in his opening address. “Open and connected markets are fundamental for such partnerships.”
Ding also called for deeper investment cooperation, greater collaboration in technological innovation, and stronger dialogue to remove trade barriers.

This year’s CIIE, the ninth annual event and the largest edition to date, welcomes a record 4,142 overseas companies from 162 countries, regions, and international organizations to Shanghai’s National Exhibition and Convention Center. The event’s total exhibition area is also its largest, exceeding 440,000 square meters.

The event, which runs Nov. 5 to 10, welcomed more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and global leading enterprises, with 2,000 companies participating for the first time. A record more than 480 products will either make their global, Asia, or China debut at the expo, including a laparoscopic surgery robot by Johnson & Johnson, a cochlear implant capable of 360-degree sound coverage by Swiss hearing care firm Advanced Bionics, and a 6G terminal prototype by U.S. tech company Qualcomm.

This year’s exhibition comprises six main sections covering technical equipment, consumer goods, food and agricultural products, automobiles and smart mobility, medical devices and health care, and trade in services. It also offers a dedicated “innovation incubation zone” for tech startups.

CIIE has also expanded efforts to support African countries, with free exhibition booth space for the “least developed” countries up 17% from last year’s exhibition. The expansion comes as China introduced zero tariffs on imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.

Launched in 2018, CIIE is the world’s first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports. The expo underlines China’s continued efforts to promote inclusive economic globalization and build an open world economy.
In the first nine months of 2026, China’s imports of foreign goods reached 16.7 trillion yuan ($2.5 trillion), up 22.3% year on year, the fastest growth since 2021, according to official data.
(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo’s exhibition center in Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. VCG)

items.title: Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019220/Double 11 Looming, Chinese Shoppers Ask Strangers to Vet Their Carts
text: Applications aimed at preventing impulse purchases have soared in popularity during this year’s Double Eleven, the world’s largest shopping festival. The apps involve users listing the items they want, along with their prices, then sharing them with friends and strangers who vote on whether they should buy them.

Dozens of such mini-programs have sprung up across major platforms including WeChat and Alipay following the August success of the WeChat mini-program “Still Want to Buy?” (Hai Mai Me in Chinese), domestic media reported last week. Related hashtags have garnered tens of millions of views on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, as of Thursday.

Domestic e-commerce giant Alibaba launched Double Eleven, also known as Singles’ Day, on Nov. 11, 2009, as a 24-hour shopping event. The festival has since grown to a monthlong event across all e-commerce platforms and begins around mid-October.

The trend comes as young Chinese consumers become increasingly money-conscious. According to a May report by Ireland-based consulting firm Accenture, 82% of the country’s Gen Z — more than 230 million people — have started saving money or cutting back on non-essential spending.

The rise in anti-impulse-buy apps dates back to the release of Still Want to Buy? in August. Created by a 29-year-old developer under the pseudonym Qiancheng, the app gained more than 75,000 daily active users within three days of its launch, and total registered users exceeded 500,000 as of mid-September. More than 85% of users are females under 24, Qiancheng told local media.

He said the tool came about after his girlfriend suggested using automated office purchase approval systems — which employees must go through to obtain authorization for work-related purchases — to govern shopping decisions. He added that he often personally feels regret after making impulse purchases.
“It’s difficult to make money nowadays, so I think it’s worth letting people we trust help us make better spending decisions,” Qiancheng said.

However, Still Want to Buy? was taken down on Oct. 31, reportedly due to targeted reporting from online trolls. Qiancheng told local media he is applying to have the mini-program relisted and is developing an independent app to expand the program’s function.
WeChat mini-program “Wait Up, Wallet” also offers similar features to Still Want to Buy?, but it allows users to seek advice from total strangers.

This October, Lin Yinjie, a 20-year-old college student from the eastern Fujian province, vibe-coded a similar app, the Alipay mini-program “Hold On a Sec.” The app lets users log items and prices and set a cooling-off period, during which friends help them decide whether to buy. So far, the program is mainly used by Lin and her friends and does not have a wide audience.

Lin told Sixth Tone that she used to place orders mindlessly while scrolling shopping apps and social media. “As a student on a tight budget, I know how easily the desire to buy things can quietly drain my wallet,” she said.

items.title: Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019222/Starbucks’ Pay-to-Sit Policy Tests ‘Third Place’ Image in China
text: For nearly 27 years, Starbucks coffeehouses in China have been a haven for non-paying patrons attracted by its comfortable seating, ample power outlets, air conditioning, and free restrooms.

This stemmed from the American company’s foundational brand concept of making its outlets “third places” — safe, accessible spaces between home and work to relax and connect with friends, whether you intend to spend or not.

In late October, Starbucks China introduced a nationwide purchase-required seating policy, pledging to be “clear in its rules but warm in its execution,” with staff encouraged to politely stop non-paying customers from hogging tables and chairs. At the same time, it unveiled plans to invest more than 300 million yuan ($45 million) in reshaping the in-store atmosphere.
As the company undergoes major corporate restructuring while continuing to expand, does it risk losing its “third place” image in China?
The first Starbucks on the Chinese mainland opened in Beijing’s World Trade Building in 1999. Today there are about 8,000 outlets across 1,100 counties in the mainland.

Li Kele regularly visits her local store in the southwestern Sichuan province. After walking in and sitting down on Oct. 21, taking a moment to browse various online platforms for discounts, Li was soon approached by a barista brandishing a menu and asking if she needed any help. “The store never used to push customers to place an order,” she says.
Starbucks outlets have been attracting non-paying patrons since the 1980s, and the company officially adopted a worldwide open-door policy in 2018.

However, concerns over disruptive behaviors, alongside the company’s desire to prioritize paying customers and staff’s experience, prompted the global headquarters to reverse the policy in January last year.
The change began at its North American stores, where a new code of conduct stated that Starbucks coffee shops, patios, restrooms, and other facilities were for employees and customers only.
Anecdotal evidence suggests baristas in China began nudging seated patrons to make purchases in early 2026.

One customer shares that in January they observed employees at a Starbucks branch in Beijing’s central Xidan shopping district walking around the store offering table service to people without drinks, which is not typically available, and promoting discount coupons. Sometimes they’d subtly point out that the store was crowded and seating was scarce.
On Oct. 19, social media users in several cities began posting about signs spotted at Starbucks stores that stated customers should “make a purchase before taking a seat.”

When a domestic media outlet contacted Starbucks China for a response that same day, a spokesperson denied any plan to introduce a purchase-required seating policy. But within 48 hours, the company made a complete U-turn, announcing that such a policy would take effect on Oct. 22.
The move has sparked much debate online. Yet in real terms, implementation has so far been limited to advisory measures, such as signage.

items.title: Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019216/Chinese App Tracking Hotel Pests Returns After Some Debugging
text: A Chinese app designed to report hotels that allegedly have bedbugs and other pests has been updated and re-released following controversy over the validity of the claims. The app attracted more than 300,000 users at its peak, flagging over 600 hotels nationwide, according to its creator.

In a Sunday post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, the creator of the app, a WeChat mini-program called “Bedbug Map,” announced that he alone would now review bedbug reports — previously, evidence was approved if a majority of users verified it. He also clarified that users are required to upload photographic evidence of bedbugs. The next day, he also posted a review of nearly 300 rejected bedbug reports, explaining why each had been declined.

Released Sept. 16, the mini-program lets users report hotels with bedbugs, cockroaches, or other pests, resulting in a bug or question mark icon over the hotel’s location. Tapping it reveals the number of user reports.

Controversy arose after reports that multiple hotels were asked by customers for refunds after they reported having found bedbugs via the app after their stay. One hotel was allegedly asked to refund 3,000 yuan ($450) in room charges after a report citing “two bumps” on a guest’s body was posted on the map and approved by users. According to the report, the hotel later asked a third party to inspect the premises, but found no traces of bedbugs.

The creator, a 26-year-old manufacturing industry worker who asked to remain anonymous, told Sixth Tone that in the past few days he had personally reviewed more than 700 pieces of photo evidence submitted over the previous two months.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone revealed that 232 hotels are now marked on the mini-program’s map, down from the more than 600 reported before Monday. The mini-program currently lists 36 hotels as having successfully appealed reports after submitting third-party evidence.
The app has also been taken down twice, most recently in late October, by WeChat parent company Tencent, citing its restrictions on applications run by and registered to individuals.

The creator told Sixth Tone that Bedbug Map was created with the help of AI in under two weeks. He said he got the idea after searching online for bedbug information after he and his girlfriend developed bites following a move, discovering most bedbug posts involved hotels.

On the day of its release, the mini-program attracted over 100,000 users, according to the creator. Under his release announcement on Xiaohongshu, many commented asking him to expand the function to public transportation, which he then added to the app. However, the function was removed in subsequent updates.
“I guess the reason the app was well-received is that it addresses a key pain point for the average traveler: the lack of cleanliness and the resurgence of bedbugs.”

items.title: Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019210/Who Gets the Credit for China’s Culinary Creations?
text: A few weeks ago, I served as a judge on a food program in China, where I met many chefs and got a close look at how they develop new dishes. I was particularly impressed by one dish: a steamed egg custard topped with a rich crab paste made from crab roe and fat. It was a combination I had never considered before. The crab paste had a delicate aroma and a rich, oily texture, while the steamed egg custard was soft and silky, perfectly balancing its richness.
I was struck by the dish’s ingenuity, but it also raised a question: Would people be willing to pay for the recipe and instructions on how to make it?

I put this question to one of the chefs on the program. He smiled at me as though I were a child and asked why anyone would pay for a recipe. He then let me in on an industry secret: When a restaurant discovers that a competitor has introduced a new dish, it will order it and have its own chefs taste it, analyze its ingredients, cooking techniques, and seasonings, and work out how it was made. In most cases, they can reproduce it. The chef told me he had recreated other people’s dishes and had his own copied by others.
It all sounded rather cutthroat. The person who bears the cost of innovation often reaps little of the reward.

In Chinese cuisine, creating a new dish is not nearly as simple as diners might imagine. Chefs must find the right ingredients, adjust proportions, experiment with different cooking temperatures, refine textures, and continually adjust based on customer feedback. Developing a successful dish can involve dozens or even hundreds of failed attempts before it is ready to serve.

The time, ingredients, and labor costs of this trial-and-error process are all borne by the original creator. Yet as soon as the dish reaches the table, anyone can observe, taste, analyze, and even reproduce it. For a competitor, learning most of the techniques needed to make a dish may cost little more than the price of a meal.

Even more frustrating, many of these innovators lack the resources to promote their creations. A small restaurant might be the first to develop a dish but lack the advertising budget, media exposure, or network of locations to popularize it. Meanwhile, a larger restaurant can simply copy the dish and quickly introduce it to a wider audience. Since more people encounter it there first, they may assume the larger restaurant came up with it.

This suggests that the first-mover advantage does not necessarily apply in the restaurant business. Being first matters only if consumers know who created the dish and the original creator has the resources and business acumen to turn that innovation into a brand and a source of revenue. Otherwise, the creator is essentially providing free research and development while introducing consumers to a dish that benefits the entire market.

items.title: China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019209/China Clears New Formula for Patients Who Must Limit Protein
text: China has approved its first domestically developed amino acid-based nutritional powder, designed to give patients with phenylketonuria (PKU) — a rare genetic disorder that affects metabolism of the amino acid phenylalanine — greater freedom in what they eat. Treatment of PKU requires lifelong dietary restrictions to prevent developmental disorders and brain damage.

The new formula officially entered the Chinese market on Oct. 30 and was jointly developed by Shanghai-based Xinhua Hospital, affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research, and dairy producer Bright Dairy.
PKU affects about one in every 11,000 newborns in China, with an estimated 120,000 to 150,000 registered patients nationwide.

Due to a genetic defect, people with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, an amino acid found in protein-rich foods. The resulting buildup can damage brain cells, requiring patients to follow a low-phenylalanine diet by cutting out meat and eating low-protein grains, while relying on milk powder-like formulas to supplement the other amino acids they need.
Earlier formulas contained 30% to 60% amino acids, with the rest composed of fats, carbohydrates, and other nutrients.

“As patients grow older, they need more protein. That means consuming more of these formulas, which also means taking in more fats and carbohydrates, increasing the risk of obesity,” Cai Wei, director of the Shanghai Institute of Pediatric Research and leader of the research team, told domestic media.

In contrast, the new formula contains 95% amino acids, allowing patients to meet their amino acid needs without consuming as much fat or as many carbohydrates, and giving them more freedom to enjoy other normal low-protein foods.

Zhuang Yingying, a 33-year-old PKU patient, told domestic media that patients previously relied heavily on imported products, and overseas supply disruptions were common. Special low-protein foods such as rice and noodles cost five to 10 times as much as regular varieties.
The formula, designed for PKU patients aged 1 and older, could save some families more than 1,000 yuan ($140) a month, according to domestic media.

Domestic PKU formulas have existed for decades, but long faced hurdles in gaining regulatory approval in China, partly because of gaps in national standards for food-grade amino acids, according to a 2020 report by domestic media outlet China Times. High registration costs and the small patient population have also discouraged manufacturers from entering the market.
China approved its first PKU medical formula in 2018, an imported product, while the first domestically produced formula received regulatory approval in 2025.

Since 2018, some parts of China, including Shanghai and neighboring Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces, have introduced public health insurance coverage for foods formulated for PKU patients. In Shanghai, annual coverage ranges from 8,000 yuan for infants under 1 to 12,000 yuan for patients over 10.

items.title: Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019198/Inside the Chinese County Selling $2 Nails to the World
text: At her desk in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai, a county in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, Chai Fenfen has hung a large print of a 100-yuan banknote.
“I came here to make money,” she says. “That’s what keeps me motivated.”

After jobs selling insurance and real estate, Chai joined the workshop in 2024. Making nails offers steady earnings and the flexibility to take her children to and from school. Workers there are paid by the piece, typically earning 3,000 to 4,000 yuan a month ($450 to $600).
But for the businesses supplying that work, the early boom has given way to fierce competition over price.

Once known for its crystal trade, Donghai used its existing e-commerce networks to build an industry around press-on nails — ready-made artificial nails that customers attach themselves. By 2024, the county had nearly 25,000 businesses in the trade, according to its press-on nail industry association.
Chai’s employer, wholesaler Li Zhifu, entered the business in 2021, and now has around 2,000 workers across his production sites and more than 20 storefronts in the county.

In the beginning, Li says, almost anything sold, regardless of color or design. Competition has since squeezed profits. He estimates that six or seven out of every 10 people who entered the trade have gone out of business.
Some businesses are competing on design, selling elaborate, handmade sets for hundreds of yuan. Others are expanding overseas sales through TikTok Shop.
As overseas orders grow, Li is experimenting with machines to make nails his workers currently produce by hand.
“For large overseas orders, consistency is key. Everything, from colors and designs to rhinestone placement, has to match,” he says. He expects machine-made nails to eventually dominate that market.
(Header image: Craftswomen work in a press-on nail workshop in Donghai County, Jiangsu province, August 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

items.title: China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019203/China’s Hit New Reality Show Shifts Focus From Love to Friendship
text: China’s latest viral reality show is about broken friendships — rather than failing romance — between celebrities.

“I Miss You” surpassed 100 million views within two days of its Oct. 22 debut, and topped the real-time TV popularity chart on Chinese review platform Douban since last Thursday. Topics related to the show have repeatedly trended on the microblogging platform Weibo since airing.
Produced by streaming platform Mango TV, the show brings together four pairs of celebrities who have reportedly fallen out for an 18-day trip through the southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region.

The show is widely seen as a riff on China’s popular relationship reality shows and follows a similar format to “See You Again,” whose fifth season aired in late 2025, which takes celebrity couples in troubled marriages on an 18-day trip before they decide whether to divorce.

In “I Miss You,” guests discuss their former friendships as a group and one-on-one with their ex-friends, play games, and share their feelings with the production team. A panel of celebrities, a psychologist, and a journalist comment on their interactions.

The most discussed pair on “I Miss You” so far has been Xu Fei and Li Na, two contestants from the 2006 season of “Super Girl,” a popular televised singing competition regarded as a cornerstone of China’s fan culture.

The two were close friends during the competition 20 years ago, but their friendship later collapsed after Li came to believe that Xu had reported her to their management company for taking outside jobs in violation of her contract. Li said the company subsequently stopped arranging work for her, which she sees as having dealt a major blow to her career. Xu denied the accusation, instead blaming a third person.
As the two revisited their past on the show, their memories of their friendship moved many viewers, with one highly upvoted comment describing their relationship as “an epic saga of love and hate.”

Xu said in tears that she had loved “wasting time together,” and noted that her current preferred snacks are the “ones Li loved back then.” Li also recalled how, even when the two appeared to be bitter enemies, they would sometimes end up crying in each other’s arms after getting drunk at gatherings.
Yet the two remained at odds over the past accusation. During an interview with the production team, Li said she had hated Xu “for a long time,” at one point shouting, “What about the money I lost?”

The other three pairs of celebrities include an actor who cut ties with a longtime producer friend after feeling pressured to accept a role, an actress and a writer who fell out when the latter grew closer to a third person, and former professional esports teammates who fought over training strategies, eventually leading one to leave the team.

“‘I Miss You’ feels so much more pure than ‘See You Again,’” read a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that received almost 3,700 likes. “In a marriage, you have to argue about more than feelings. There’s property, children, parents, and so much else. With friendship, we can sit down and focus on just one thing: how we feel about each other.”
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China's services trade rises 8.5% in first nine months of 2026, deficit narrows
text: China's services trade grew 8.5 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, with the trade deficit narrowing and transport services leading growth, official data showed on Wednesday, as the country steps up efforts to foster new growth drivers in the services sector.

The sustained expansion reflects a broader shift toward higher-value services, as China's vast manufacturing base and industrial upgrading open new opportunities in international markets and deepen the integration of manufacturing and modern services, analysts said.

According to the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), China's services trade reached 5.77 trillion yuan ($863.7 billion) during the January-September period. Exports rose 14.8 percent to 2.27 trillion yuan, outpacing a 4.8 percent increase in imports. The services trade deficit narrowed by 132.66 billion yuan from a year earlier to 1.23 trillion yuan.

Transport services led all categories in trade growth, with combined imports and exports surging 33.9 percent to 1.28 trillion yuan, making it China's third-largest services trade category after travel and other business services.

Knowledge-intensive services also maintained solid growth. Trade in the category rose 7.4 percent in the first nine months. Exports climbed 11.7 percent to 1.22 trillion yuan, making up 53.7 percent of total services exports. Personal, cultural and recreational services posted the fastest rate of export growth at 69.1 percent, followed by insurance and pension services at 50.3 percent.

Song Ding, a senior research fellow at the Shenzhen-based China Development Institute, described the narrowing trade deficit as an encouraging development, pointing to China's growing services export capacity and international competitiveness.

"When manufacturing reaches a certain level of development, especially on the scale seen in China, moving further up the value chain and expanding into modern services becomes a natural progression," Song told the Global Times on Wednesday.
This shift is also evident in the growing links between China's manufacturing exports and international transport services, Song said.

"As Chinese-made goods reach more overseas markets, domestic companies are expanding their presence in shipping, rail freight and air cargo networks, rather than relying solely on foreign operators to handle international deliveries."

The momentum is also evident in China's broader services sector. China's services sector expanded 5.2 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters, outpacing overall GDP growth of 4.6 percent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). The sector contributed 66.3 percent of economic growth, up 5.6 percentage points from a year earlier.

At an October 19 press briefing, NBS Deputy Commissioner Mao Shengyong highlighted the accelerating integration of advanced manufacturing and modern services, with industrial chains moving toward more specialized, higher-value activities. He also identified artificial intelligence as a key driver of growth in the information technology-related sector.

Pope Leo: Church in China shows unity is communion in diversity
text: Pope Leo XIV sent a video message on Thursday to an international conference entitled “The Face of the Universal Church in China: 100 Years Since the Consecration of the First Chinese Bishops.”
Taking place in Rome, the conference was organized by the Dicastery for Evangelization – Section for First Evangelization, in collaboration with the Pontifical Urbaniana University.

In his message, the Pope recalled the first six Chinese Catholic Bishops consecrated in modern times, and their journey from Shanghai to Rome to receive episcopal ordination in St. Peter’s Basilica at the hands of Pope Pius XI on October 28, 1926.
“Their consecration was an event of great significance, not only for the journey of the Catholic Church in China but also for the universal Church,” he said.
Pope Leo pointed to Pope Benedict XV’s 1919 apostolic letter Maximum illud, which affirmed that the Church’s missionary work must not be confused with colonization or cultural imposition.
The Gospel, he said, grows wherever it is sown through the grace of God, not through human strategies.

“The Church, which is born of mission and the first proclamation of the Gospel,” he added, “is happy to take on the characteristics and nuances of the people and nations among whom she is called to bear witness to Christ in charity.”

At the first General Council of the Church in China—the Council of Shanghai in 1924—the Church expressed the urgent desire to entrust leadership of local communities to native-born Chinese priests and Bishops.
“It was necessary to initiate and foster that process in order to remain faithful to the very nature of the Church, whose unity is not uniformity but communion in diversity,” said Pope Leo.

The Catholic faith embraces the differences and—wherever possible—the characteristics of individuals and peoples in every culture, he noted, recalling that this aspect mirrors God’s way of calling each person with their unique qualities.
“The Church lives among the peoples with friendship and sympathy for their hopes and noble aspirations,” he said.

Recalling the missionary Bishop St. Toribio de Mogrovejo, Pope Leo said each Bishop receives and carries out the mission in communion with the Successor of Peter and other Bishops spread throughout the world.
He said the six Chinese Bishops consecrated in 1926 crossed the globe “to bear witness to the communion that blossoms from the faith of the Apostles,” in communion with the Bishop of Rome.

“It is a beautiful, gratuitous, and comforting sign; a liberating bond; a closeness that instills confidence; and above all, a manifestation of the mystery of the Mystical Body of Christ,” said Pope Leo.

He noted with Pope Benedict XVI and Pope Francis that the Catholic Church in China has never been deprived of the “ministry of legitimate shepherds who have preserved the apostolic succession intact.”

Pope Leo XIV concluded his video message by recalling the “joy and pride” which the consecration of the six Bishops kindled in Chinese Catholics, saying the event consigned “mistrust, suspicion, and hostility to oblivion.”
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China’s Economics of Denial
text: Oliver Melton is a Director with Rhodium Group’s China practice.

Logan Wright is a Partner at Rhodium Group and leads its research on China’s economy and financial markets. He is the author of the book Broken China: How the Economic Miracle Shattered and What it Means for the World.
Beijing’s Theory of Success in the Face of Failure

China has correctly diagnosed its most pressing economic problems. The Chinese Communist Party has acknowledged that its economy relies too much on investment and exports and that persistently weak household consumption is the core threat to future growth. The leadership also knows that this imbalanced growth model is causing trade friction with developed and emerging economies alike and will continue to do so. They know there is a growing chorus of economists (including many quiet voices in China) raising the alarm that, if Beijing does not make major changes soon, China will face ever-slower growth, cascading trade disputes, and potentially stagnating household income.

But what is puzzling is that the country’s leaders are not acting. Beijing has announced only modest plans to boost household consumption and domestic demand, and its overall economic strategy remains essentially unchanged—focused on expanding investment in manufacturing, especially in advanced technologies and new strategic industries.

Theories abound as to why Beijing has chosen to ignore the warnings. Many speculate that Chinese leader Xi Jinping is not receiving accurate information or that he and his closest allies have abandoned development as a priority in favor of national security goals or a desire to control the commanding heights of global industry. Others argue that Beijing knows what it should do, but political or institutional constraints prevent it from taking decisive action.

In truth, while these factors all play a part in shaping policy, the real explanation is far simpler. The party is sticking to this path because the leadership believes it is working. It sees the same troubling data—including rising external surpluses, weak consumption, slower household income growth, weak credit demand, rising unemployment and underemployment, and persistent deflation—but it has reached wildly different conclusions about what these developments indicate and what Beijing should do in response.
